````
# amail: email as a Copilot control surface

Status: initial design for discussion
Date: 2026-09-02

## Problem

Copilot can keep working without attention, but its useful stopping points still require a person to return to the terminal:

- it needs one or more answers;
- it encounters an error or cannot continue;
- it finishes a task and has a result to review;
- it is idle and can accept another instruction.

`amail` makes email a small control surface for those transitions. It should send a useful, human-readable message rather than exposing raw hook or API payloads. A reply should become input to the same Copilot session.

## Take-home constraints

This should be a modest tool that can be completed and demonstrated in 3-5 hours.

The design therefore favors:

- Copilot CLI only for the first version;
- one local user and one configured email address;
- a CLI/demo workflow rather than a web UI;
- Resend's managed receiving domain and polling API, avoiding deployed webhook infrastructure;
- a project-level Copilot CLI extension attached to the foreground interactive session;
- one agent-callable `ask_human_by_email` tool instead of intercepting native `ask_user`;
- the agent's own final response as the completion summary, rather than another model call.

Not in the MVP: native `ask_user` interception, structured elicitation, IDE integration, Copilot cloud agent support, multiple users, attachments, rich HTML composition, arbitrary email commands, or a hosted service.

## Agreed MVP decisions

- Target Copilot CLI only.
- Preserve the standard interactive Copilot TUI rather than replacing it with `-p`, ACP, or a custom frontend.
- Automatically enqueue an authorized email reply into the same foreground session.
- Use a Resend-managed receiving address.
- Wait for answers while Copilot and its extension remain running, unless the turn is cancelled or the request expires after 24 hours.
- Keep undelivered follow-up replies durable if the extension temporarily disconnects.

## Proposed user experience

Start Copilot normally in the repository:

```text
copilot
```

The project extension automatically joins the foreground session. The user works in the ordinary terminal UI and can step away at any point.

### When Copilot needs input

Project instructions tell Copilot to use the extension's `ask_human_by_email` tool instead of native `ask_user` when the user may be away. The tool sends one or more questions and waits for an authorized reply.

```text
Subject: [amail] Input needed: Add pagination to the issue list

Copilot needs your input

1. Which pagination style should I implement?
   - Previous/next links
   - Page numbers
   - Infinite scroll

Context:
The existing API accepts page and per_page.

Reply with your answer. You can also include additional instructions.
```

The tool returns the cleaned reply body to Copilot, preserving the same interactive turn. The model, rather than a brittle email parser, interprets answers to multiple questions and any additional instruction.

### When Copilot fails

The extension observes root-session errors and sends the error category, a concise message, and the current task/session identity. Stack traces stay out of email by default. Recoverability is derived conservatively from the error type rather than claimed as an SDK-provided field.

A reply is queued as the next instruction for that session after it becomes idle. It does not execute as a shell command.

### When Copilot needs permission

The extension handles permission requests while the user is away. The email includes the permission kind and exact command or resource. Only an exact first-line `APPROVE` or `DENY` is accepted; freeform text cannot approve a tool call.

If the permission request is cancelled, superseded, or the extension disconnects, the email token is expired and a late reply cannot authorize a different operation.

### When Copilot completes

When the extension observes a root-agent assistant response followed by a non-aborted `session.idle`, the user receives the response, repository, elapsed time, and changed files from `git status --porcelain`. For the MVP, "complete" means the current top-level turn is idle; it does not mean the interactive CLI process has exited.

```text
Subject: [amail] Complete: Add pagination to the issue list

Copilot completed the task.

Repository: Qworg/amail

Implemented previous/next pagination, preserved the current filters,
and added request and UI coverage.

Changed:
- src/issues/list.ts
- src/issues/list.test.ts

Reply with another instruction to resume this Copilot session.
```

Replying causes the extension to call `session.send()` and enqueue the reply as the next prompt in the same foreground session. The next idle turn produces another email in the same thread.

## Why a foreground extension

Copilot CLI extensions run as child processes and call `joinSession()` to attach to the current foreground session. The joined session can:

- register an agent-callable tool and a permission callback;
- subscribe to root assistant, error, idle, user-message, and shutdown events;
- call `session.send()` to inject a new user message into the same session.

This is a better fit than intercepting terminal input or starting a second Copilot process. It preserves the standard TUI and gives the integration structured events rather than screen-scraped text.

The extension API is experimental and version-sensitive. The take-home should pin and demonstrate the installed Copilot CLI version (`1.0.83-3`) rather than present this as a production-stable integration.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph cli["Copilot CLI"]
        tui["Standard interactive TUI"]
        session["Foreground session"]
        extension["amail-bridge extension"]
        tui <--> session
        extension <-->|"joinSession JSON-RPC"| session
    end

    daemon["amail daemon"]
    resend["Resend APIs"]
    inbox["User email inbox"]

    extension -->|"question, permission, error, idle summary"| daemon
    daemon -->|"answer, decision, or queued prompt"| extension
    daemon -->|"send notification"| resend
    resend -->|"delivered email"| inbox
    inbox -->|"user reply"| resend
    resend -->|"poll received mail"| daemon
```

### Copilot extension

The project contains `.github/extensions/amail-bridge/extension.mjs`.

Its agent-facing contract is intentionally small:

```ts
ask_human_by_email({
  subject: string,
  questions: Array<{
    question: string,
    choices?: string[]
  }>,
  context?: string
}): {
  reply: string
}
```

The extension:

- calls `joinSession()` and records the foreground `sessionId`;
- registers `ask_human_by_email({ subject, questions, context })`;
- implements `onPermissionRequest` with exact `APPROVE`/`DENY` replies;
- subscribes to root `assistant.message`, `user.message`, `session.idle`, `session.error`, and session shutdown events;
- sends normalized events to the daemon over an owner-only Windows named pipe;
- polls or receives queued replies from the daemon;
- returns answers through the pending tool or permission callback;
- calls `session.send({ prompt, mode: "enqueue" })` for follow-up instructions received after idle.

The extension advertises the email tool to the agent; this makes `amail` an agent interface rather than passive notification plumbing. Project instructions tell the agent when to choose it.

The extension does not receive the Resend API key. Its stdout is reserved for the Copilot JSON-RPC transport, so diagnostics go through the extension logging API or stderr. It logs every injected email prompt into the visible Copilot timeline.

### Local daemon

The daemon is the single owner of mutable state and the Resend client.

Responsibilities:

- send question, failure, and completion emails;
- poll Resend's received-email list and retrieve new message bodies;
- correlate replies using an opaque token in the reply-to address;
- resolve a pending tool or permission request, or enqueue a new session prompt;
- deliver at most one reply at a time to each connected extension;
- suppress duplicate events and inbound messages;
- persist a small amount of routing state to survive a restart.

For the take-home, the daemon owns one atomically replaced JSON state file under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\amail\`. Only routing metadata is persisted:

```text
sessions: session ID, cwd, bridge connection ID, status
requests: request ID, session ID, kind, token hash, status, expiry, outbound message ID
seenInbound: Resend message ID and timestamp
```

Full email bodies are not persisted. State-file access is restricted to the current Windows user.

The daemon may restart independently. If the extension disconnects, follow-up instructions remain queued. Pending tool and permission requests are cancelled because their original callbacks no longer exist. Automatic delivery requires the exact matching interactive Copilot session and extension connection; the daemon must not start a competing `--resume` process.

### Resend integration

Outbound mail uses the existing `RESEND_API_KEY` from `../.env`.

Inbound mail uses a Resend-managed receiving domain for setup speed. The daemon polls the Received Emails API every few seconds, then retrieves the full plain-text body for unseen messages. This avoids requiring a public webhook during the demo; a webhook can replace polling without changing the routing model.

Each message uses a reply-to address such as:

```text
reply+<opaque-token>@<resend-managed-domain>
```

Tokens use at least 128 random bits encoded as lowercase base32. Each token is single-use, expires after 24 hours, and is scoped to one request kind: question, permission, or follow-up. A question or permission token can never become a general follow-up prompt.

Routing depends on the token rather than subject text. A reply must also reference the recorded outbound message ID through `In-Reply-To`; `Re:` subjects are used for best-effort visual threading. Outbound mail sets `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated`. Inbound auto-replies and list mail are rejected.

Inbound authorization treats the token as the primary capability and an exact parsed sender-address match as defense in depth. If Resend exposes SPF, DKIM, or DMARC verdicts, failed authentication is rejected; this must be verified before implementation.

Before delivery, the daemon removes quoted history and signatures, rejects forwarded-message markers, caps the body at 4 KB, and wraps it as explicitly user-authored email content. Message content and routing tokens transit Resend and may be visible in its dashboard; this is disclosed in the README.

## State machine

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR

    [*] --> Idle

    Idle --> Running: terminal prompt
    Idle --> DeliveryPending: authorized follow-up email
    DeliveryPending --> Running: matching user.message confirms delivery
    DeliveryPending --> Idle: delivery rejected or cancelled

    Running --> WaitingForHuman: ask_human_by_email
    Running --> WaitingForPermission: permission requested
    WaitingForHuman --> Running: authorized answer
    WaitingForPermission --> Running: APPROVE or DENY
    WaitingForHuman --> Interrupted: cancelled, expired, or disconnected
    WaitingForPermission --> Interrupted: cancelled, expired, or disconnected

    Running --> Idle: root session.idle
    Running --> Interrupted: aborted root session.idle
    Interrupted --> Idle: interruption email recorded

    Idle --> SessionEnded: CLI exits
    Running --> SessionEnded: CLI exits
    SessionEnded --> [*]
```

Only one delivery may be pending per session. The daemon marks an email delivered only after observing the corresponding root `user.message`; otherwise it remains queued or is rejected explicitly.

## Alternatives considered

| Approach | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Native `ask_user` interception | Reject | The TUI and extension race to resolve the same pending request, variant selection is session-level, and reload can orphan the callback. |
| Config hooks only | Reject | Hooks can notify or make an immediate decision, but cannot durably return an email answer hours later. |
| Start `copilot --resume` beside the open CLI | Reject | Concurrent access has no session locking and can create competing owners with stale or interleaved state. |
| ACP client | Reject for this MVP | ACP can own or restore a session, but cannot attach to the existing TUI process. |
| `/remote` | Useful fallback | It controls the live CLI through GitHub web/mobile, but exposes no supported custom email-service API. |
| ConPTY/`node-pty` wrapper | Reject unless extensions fail | It preserves the TUI and permits input injection, but adds terminal-hosting and screen-stream complexity that the extension API avoids. |
| Foreground CLI extension | Choose | It joins the exact interactive session and exposes native callbacks, structured events, and `session.send()`. |

## Trust and safety boundaries

- Accept inbound instructions only from the configured email address.
- Use high-entropy, single-use, kind-scoped routing tokens and store only SHA-256 hashes.
- Consume a pending token atomically before acting on its reply.
- Treat email bodies as untrusted input, never as shell syntax or CLI flags.
- Deliver replies only through native callback results or `session.send()`; never construct a shell command from a reply.
- Do not include environment variables, raw transcripts, tool outputs, or stack traces in outgoing mail.
- Truncate and redact common credential patterns from the latest root assistant response before emailing it.
- Ignore attachments in the MVP.
- Record Resend message IDs to make inbound processing idempotent.
- Reject auto-responders, forwarded content, and replies that do not match the expected outbound `Message-ID`.
- Use an owner-only Windows named pipe rather than a loopback TCP port.
- Keep `RESEND_API_KEY` in the daemon; do not request or pass it into the extension process.
- Launch the daemon explicitly with a send-scoped Resend key; never log the key.
- Support a daemon-level `STOP` command that disables notifications and queued delivery without involving the model.
- Cap automatic follow-up turns per session to prevent mail loops.

## Failure behavior

- Resend send failure: persist the notification and retry with bounded backoff; surface the failure in the local CLI.
- Inbound polling failure: keep the Copilot request waiting and show daemon health locally.
- Unknown or expired reply token: do not route the message; log a concise rejection.
- Duplicate reply: acknowledge only the first delivery with that Resend message ID.
- Copilot still running a turn: use `session.send()` in its default enqueue mode rather than implementing another queue in the extension.
- Tool or permission request cancelled: atomically expire its token; a late reply is rejected rather than converted into a new prompt.
- Extension reload: cancel pending tool and permission requests; keep only standalone follow-up instructions queued for the matching session.
- CLI exit: keep the reply queued, but require the user to resume an interactive session; do not start a competing Copilot process automatically.
- Daemon restart: restore routing metadata, continue polling from persisted message IDs, and let the extension reconnect.
- Root idle with `aborted: true`: send an "Interrupted" message, never a "Complete" message.
- Sub-agent events: ignore them for completion email purposes.
- Autopilot mode: do not offer email question handling because Copilot may auto-answer user-input requests.

## Suggested implementation slice

1. Prove Resend send and receive with the configured account before building the integration.
2. Load a minimal project extension, call `joinSession()`, and exchange a named-pipe health message with the daemon.
3. Send a root-idle completion email and inject its reply with `session.send()`.
4. Add `ask_human_by_email`, reusing the same token and reply path.
5. Add email permission approval, reusing the request state machine with stricter reply parsing.
6. Add pure-function tests for token consumption, sender/thread validation, body cleaning, and duplicate message IDs.
7. Add `--simulate-inbound` so the end-to-end demo is not wholly dependent on email delivery timing.

The daemon, extension, state file, and Resend adapter are the whole product. No UI, generic MCP server, SQLite layer, webhook deployment, transcript summarizer, or retry framework is included.

## Important unknowns to validate early

- Whether the project extension is enabled and approved in a clean Copilot CLI startup.
- Exact `onPermissionRequest` response shapes for the permission kinds used in the demo.
- How cancellation is surfaced to an in-flight extension tool and permission callback.
- Whether the Resend account already has a receiving address/domain enabled.
- Whether the configured Resend account can send to the chosen recipient.
- Which inbound sender-authentication results Resend exposes.
- Which headers Resend preserves for inbound and outbound threading.

## Remaining implementation inputs

- The authorized recipient/sender email address.
- Whether every idle top-level turn should generate email. The current recommendation is yes while the project extension is enabled, because that is the explicit opt-in boundary.

## Demo preflight

- Start the daemon explicitly with its configuration and confirm the extension can connect to its named pipe.
- Start ordinary interactive `copilot` in the repository and confirm `amail-bridge` is loaded before walking away.
- Confirm the signed-in Resend account can send to and receive from the configured address.
- Use a narrow Copilot tool-permission policy; do not run the demo with blanket approval.
- Rehearse both real inbound mail and `--simulate-inbound`.

## Primary references

- Copilot CLI extensions overview: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/copilot-cli/about-cli-extensions
- Installed extension SDK documentation: `copilot-sdk/docs/extensions.md`
- Installed extension SDK examples: `copilot-sdk/docs/examples.md`
- GitHub Copilot hooks reference: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference
- GitHub Copilot CLI command reference: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-command-reference
- Resend receiving introduction: https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/receiving/introduction
- Resend list received emails API: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/emails/list-received-emails
- Resend retrieve received email API: https://resend.com/docs/api-reference/emails/retrieve-received-email
````

````
# Copilot CLI Extensions

Extensions add custom tools, hooks, and behaviors to the Copilot CLI. They run as separate Node.js processes that communicate with the CLI over JSON-RPC via stdio.

## How Extensions Work

```
┌─────────────────────┐          JSON-RPC / stdio           ┌──────────────────────┐
│   Copilot CLI        │ ◄──────────────────────────────────► │  Extension Process   │
│   (parent process)   │    tool calls, events, hooks        │  (forked child)      │
│                      │                                      │                      │
│  • Discovers exts    │                                      │  • Registers tools   │
│  • Forks processes   │                                      │  • Registers hooks   │
│  • Routes tool calls │                                      │  • Listens to events │
│  • Manages lifecycle │                                      │  • Uses SDK APIs     │
└─────────────────────┘                                      └──────────────────────┘
```

1. **Discovery**: The CLI scans `.github/extensions/` (project) and the user's copilot config extensions directory for subdirectories containing `extension.mjs`.
2. **Launch**: Each extension is forked as a child process with `@github/copilot-sdk` available via an automatic module resolver.
3. **Connection**: The extension calls `joinSession()` which establishes a JSON-RPC connection over stdio to the CLI and attaches to the user's current foreground session.
4. **Registration**: Tools and hooks declared in the session options are registered with the CLI and become available to the agent.
5. **Lifecycle**: Extensions are reloaded on `/clear` (or if the foreground session is replaced) and stopped on CLI exit (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5s).

## File Structure

```
.github/extensions/
  my-extension/
    extension.mjs      ← Entry point (required, must be .mjs)
```

- Only `.mjs` files are supported (ES modules). The file must be named `extension.mjs`.
- Each extension lives in its own subdirectory.
- The `@github/copilot-sdk` import is resolved automatically — you don't install it.

## The SDK

Extensions use `@github/copilot-sdk` for all interactions with the CLI:

```js
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const session = await joinSession({
    tools: [
        /* ... */
    ],
    hooks: {
        /* ... */
    },
});
```

The `session` object provides methods for sending messages, logging to the timeline, listening to events, and accessing the RPC API. See the `.d.ts` files in the SDK package for full type information.

## Requesting Sensitive Environment Variables

The CLI strips sensitive environment variables (for example `GITHUB_TOKEN`) from every extension process before it starts. An extension that needs one asks for it by name:

```js
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const session = await joinSession({
    requestedEnvironmentVariables: ["GITHUB_TOKEN"],
});

// Granted values are in process.env once joinSession resolves.
const token = process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN;
```

The CLI prompts the user with the extension's name and the exact list of variables requested. If the user approves, only those variables reach this extension and their values are written into `process.env` before `joinSession()` resolves. If the user denies, `joinSession()` rejects, the extension does not load, and its tools never reach the model.

An approval is remembered against the exact set of names the user saw, so an extension that later asks for an additional variable prompts again. Names that are unset, or that the CLI does not filter from extensions, are not prompted for.

An approved extension can pass a granted value to anything it starts, so ask only for what the extension genuinely needs.

## Further Reading

- `examples.md` — Practical code examples for tools, hooks, events, and complete extensions
- `factories.md`: Authoring, running, resuming, and observing Agent Factories
- `agent-author.md` — Step-by-step workflow for agents authoring extensions programmatically
````

````
# Copilot CLI Extension Examples

A practical guide to writing extensions using the `@github/copilot-sdk` extension API.

## Extension Skeleton

Every extension starts with the same boilerplate:

```js
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const session = await joinSession({
    hooks: {
        /* ... */
    },
    tools: [
        /* ... */
    ],
});
```

`joinSession` returns a `CopilotSession` object you can use to send messages and subscribe to events.

> **Platform notes (Windows vs macOS/Linux):**
>
> - Use `process.platform === "win32"` to detect Windows at runtime.
> - Clipboard: `pbcopy` on macOS, `clip` on Windows.
> - Use `exec()` instead of `execFile()` for `.cmd` scripts like `code`, `npx`, `npm` on Windows.
> - PowerShell stderr redirection uses `*>&1` instead of `2>&1`.

---

## Logging to the Timeline

Use `session.log()` to surface messages to the user in the CLI timeline:

```js
const session = await joinSession({
    hooks: {
        onSessionStart: async () => {
            await session.log("My extension loaded");
        },
        onPreToolUse: async (input) => {
            if (input.toolName === "bash") {
                await session.log(`Running: ${input.toolArgs?.command}`, { ephemeral: true });
            }
        },
    },
    tools: [],
});
```

Levels: `"info"` (default), `"warning"`, `"error"`. Set `ephemeral: true` for transient messages that aren't persisted.

---

## Registering Custom Tools

Tools are functions the agent can call. Define them with a name, description, JSON Schema parameters, and a handler.

### Basic tool

```js
tools: [
    {
        name: "my_tool",
        description: "Does something useful",
        parameters: {
            type: "object",
            properties: {
                input: { type: "string", description: "The input value" },
            },
            required: ["input"],
        },
        handler: async (args) => {
            return `Processed: ${args.input}`;
        },
    },
];
```

### Tool that invokes an external shell command

```js
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";

{
    name: "run_command",
    description: "Runs a shell command and returns its output",
    parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
            command: { type: "string", description: "The command to run" },
        },
        required: ["command"],
    },
    handler: async (args) => {
        const isWindows = process.platform === "win32";
        const shell = isWindows ? "powershell" : "bash";
        const shellArgs = isWindows
            ? ["-NoProfile", "-Command", args.command]
            : ["-c", args.command];
        return new Promise((resolve) => {
            execFile(shell, shellArgs, (err, stdout, stderr) => {
                if (err) resolve(`Error: ${stderr || err.message}`);
                else resolve(stdout);
            });
        });
    },
}
```

### Tool that calls an external API

```js
{
    name: "fetch_data",
    description: "Fetches data from an API endpoint",
    parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
            url: { type: "string", description: "The URL to fetch" },
        },
        required: ["url"],
    },
    handler: async (args) => {
        const res = await fetch(args.url);
        if (!res.ok) return `Error: HTTP ${res.status}`;
        return await res.text();
    },
}
```

### Tool handler invocation context

The handler receives a second argument with invocation metadata:

```js
handler: async (args, invocation) => {
    // invocation.sessionId  — current session ID
    // invocation.toolCallId — unique ID for this tool call
    // invocation.toolName   — name of the tool being called
    return "done";
};
```

---

## Hooks

Hooks intercept and modify behavior at key lifecycle points. Register them in the `hooks` option.

### Available Hooks

| Hook                    | Fires When                               | Can Modify                                  |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `onUserPromptSubmitted` | User sends a message                     | The prompt text, add context                |
| `onPreToolUse`          | Before a tool executes                   | Tool args, permission decision, add context |
| `onPostToolUse`         | After a tool executes successfully       | Tool result, add context                    |
| `onPostToolUseFailure`  | After a tool execution returns a failure | Add hidden guidance to the model            |
| `onSessionStart`        | Session starts or resumes                | Add context                                 |
| `onSessionEnd`          | Session ends                             | Cleanup actions, summary                    |
| `onErrorOccurred`       | An error occurs                          | Error handling strategy (retry/skip/abort)  |

All hook inputs include `timestamp` (`Date`) and `workingDirectory`.

### Modifying the user's message

Use `onUserPromptSubmitted` to rewrite or augment what the user typed before the agent sees it.

```js
hooks: {
    onUserPromptSubmitted: async (input) => {
        // Rewrite the prompt
        return { modifiedPrompt: input.prompt.toUpperCase() };
    },
}
```

### Injecting additional context into every message

Return `additionalContext` to silently append instructions the agent will follow.

```js
hooks: {
    onUserPromptSubmitted: async (input) => {
        return {
            additionalContext: "Always respond in bullet points. Follow our team coding standards.",
        };
    },
}
```

### Sending a follow-up message based on a keyword

Use `session.send()` to programmatically inject a new user message.

```js
hooks: {
    onUserPromptSubmitted: async (input) => {
        if (/\\burgent\\b/i.test(input.prompt)) {
            // Fire-and-forget a follow-up message
            setTimeout(() => session.send({ prompt: "Please prioritize this." }), 0);
        }
    },
}
```

> **Tip:** Guard against infinite loops if your follow-up message could re-trigger the same hook.

### Blocking dangerous tool calls

Use `onPreToolUse` to inspect and optionally deny tool execution.

```js
hooks: {
    onPreToolUse: async (input) => {
        if (input.toolName === "bash") {
            const cmd = String(input.toolArgs?.command || "");
            if (/rm\\s+-rf/i.test(cmd) || /Remove-Item\\s+.*-Recurse/i.test(cmd)) {
                return {
                    permissionDecision: "deny",
                    permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive commands are not allowed.",
                };
            }
        }
        // Allow everything else
        return { permissionDecision: "allow" };
    },
}
```

### Modifying tool arguments before execution

```js
hooks: {
    onPreToolUse: async (input) => {
        if (input.toolName === "bash") {
            const redirect = process.platform === "win32" ? "*>&1" : "2>&1";
            return {
                modifiedArgs: {
                    ...input.toolArgs,
                    command: `${input.toolArgs.command} ${redirect}`,
                },
            };
        }
    },
}
```

### Reacting when the agent creates or edits a file

Use `onPostToolUse` to run side effects after a tool completes.

```js
import { exec } from "node:child_process";

hooks: {
    onPostToolUse: async (input) => {
        if (input.toolName === "create" || input.toolName === "edit") {
            const filePath = input.toolArgs?.path;
            if (filePath) {
                // Open the file in VS Code
                exec(`code "${filePath}"`, () => {});
            }
        }
    },
}
```

### Reacting when a tool fails

`onPostToolUse` only fires for successful tool executions. To observe or react
to failures, register `onPostToolUseFailure`. The input includes
`input.error` (the stringified failure message); only `additionalContext` on
the return value is consumed by the runtime, and it is appended as hidden
guidance alongside the failed tool result.

```js
hooks: {
    onPostToolUseFailure: async (input) => {
        if (input.toolName === "bash") {
            return {
                additionalContext: "The command failed. Try a different approach.",
            };
        }
    },
}
```

### Running a linter after every file edit

```js
import { exec } from "node:child_process";

hooks: {
    onPostToolUse: async (input) => {
        if (input.toolName === "edit") {
            const filePath = input.toolArgs?.path;
            if (filePath?.endsWith(".ts")) {
                const result = await new Promise((resolve) => {
                    exec(`npx eslint "${filePath}"`, (err, stdout) => {
                        resolve(err ? stdout : "No lint errors.");
                    });
                });
                return { additionalContext: `Lint result: ${result}` };
            }
        }
    },
}
```

### Handling errors with retry logic

```js
hooks: {
    onErrorOccurred: async (input) => {
        if (input.recoverable && input.errorContext === "model_call") {
            return { errorHandling: "retry", retryCount: 2 };
        }
        return {
            errorHandling: "abort",
            userNotification: `An error occurred: ${input.error}`,
        };
    },
}
```

### Session lifecycle hooks

```js
hooks: {
    onSessionStart: async (input) => {
        // input.source is "startup", "resume", or "new"
        return { additionalContext: "Remember to write tests for all changes." };
    },
    onSessionEnd: async (input) => {
        // input.reason is "complete", "error", "abort", "timeout", or "user_exit"
    },
}
```

---

## Session Events

After calling `joinSession`, use `session.on()` to react to events in real time.

### Listening to a specific event type

```js
session.on("assistant.message", (event) => {
    // event.data.content has the agent's response text
});
```

### Listening to all events

```js
session.on((event) => {
    // event.type and event.data are available for all events
});
```

### Unsubscribing from events

`session.on()` returns an unsubscribe function:

```js
const unsubscribe = session.on("tool.execution_complete", (event) => {
    // event.data.success, event.data.result, event.data.error
});

// Later, stop listening
unsubscribe();
```

### Example: Auto-copy agent responses to clipboard

Combine a hook (to detect a keyword) with a session event (to capture the response):

```js
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";

let copyNextResponse = false;

function copyToClipboard(text) {
    const cmd = process.platform === "win32" ? "clip" : "pbcopy";
    const proc = execFile(cmd, [], () => {});
    proc.stdin.write(text);
    proc.stdin.end();
}

const session = await joinSession({
    hooks: {
        onUserPromptSubmitted: async (input) => {
            if (/\\bcopy\\b/i.test(input.prompt)) {
                copyNextResponse = true;
            }
        },
    },
    tools: [],
});

session.on("assistant.message", (event) => {
    if (copyNextResponse) {
        copyNextResponse = false;
        copyToClipboard(event.data.content);
    }
});
```

### Top 10 Most Useful Event Types

| Event Type                  | Description                                      | Key Data Fields                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `assistant.message`         | Agent's final response                           | `content`, `messageId`, `toolRequests`                 |
| `assistant.message_delta`   | Message content chunks (ephemeral)               | `deltaContent`                                         |
| `tool.execution_start`      | A tool is about to run                           | `toolCallId`, `toolName`, `arguments`                  |
| `tool.execution_complete`   | A tool finished running                          | `toolCallId`, `success`, `result`, `error`             |
| `user.message`              | User sent a message                              | `content`, `attachments`, `source`                     |
| `session.idle`              | Session finished processing a turn               | `aborted`                                              |
| `session.error`             | An error occurred                                | `errorType`, `message`, `stack`                        |
| `permission.requested`      | Agent needs permission (shell, file write, etc.) | `requestId`, `permissionRequest.kind`                  |
| `session.shutdown`          | Session is ending                                | `shutdownType`, `totalPremiumRequests`, `codeChanges`  |
| `assistant.turn_start`      | Agent begins a new thinking/response cycle       | `turnId`                                               |

### Example: Detecting when the plan file is created or edited

Use `session.workspacePath` to locate the session's `plan.md`, then `fs.watchFile` to detect changes.
Correlate `tool.execution_start` / `tool.execution_complete` events by `toolCallId` to distinguish agent edits from user edits.

```js
import { existsSync, watchFile, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const agentEdits = new Set(); // toolCallIds for in-flight agent edits
const recentAgentPaths = new Set(); // paths recently written by the agent

const session = await joinSession();

const workspace = session.workspacePath; // e.g. ~/.copilot/session-state/<id>
if (workspace) {
    const planPath = join(workspace, "plan.md");
    let lastContent = existsSync(planPath) ? readFileSync(planPath, "utf-8") : null;

    // Track agent edits to suppress false triggers
    session.on("tool.execution_start", (event) => {
        if (
            (event.data.toolName === "edit" || event.data.toolName === "create") &&
            String(event.data.arguments?.path || "").endsWith("plan.md")
        ) {
            agentEdits.add(event.data.toolCallId);
            recentAgentPaths.add(planPath);
        }
    });
    session.on("tool.execution_complete", (event) => {
        if (agentEdits.delete(event.data.toolCallId)) {
            setTimeout(() => {
                recentAgentPaths.delete(planPath);
                lastContent = existsSync(planPath) ? readFileSync(planPath, "utf-8") : null;
            }, 2000);
        }
    });

    watchFile(planPath, { interval: 1000 }, () => {
        if (recentAgentPaths.has(planPath) || agentEdits.size > 0) return;
        const content = existsSync(planPath) ? readFileSync(planPath, "utf-8") : null;
        if (content === lastContent) return;
        const wasCreated = lastContent === null && content !== null;
        lastContent = content;
        if (content !== null) {
            session.send({
                prompt: `The plan was ${wasCreated ? "created" : "edited"} by the user.`,
            });
        }
    });
}
```

### Example: Reacting when the user manually edits any file in the repo

Use `fs.watch` with `recursive: true` on `process.cwd()` to detect file changes.
Filter out agent edits by tracking `tool.execution_start` / `tool.execution_complete` events.

```js
import { watch, readFileSync, statSync } from "node:fs";
import { join, relative, resolve } from "node:path";
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const agentEditPaths = new Set();

const session = await joinSession();

const cwd = process.cwd();
const IGNORE = new Set(["node_modules", ".git", "dist"]);

// Track agent file edits
session.on("tool.execution_start", (event) => {
    if (event.data.toolName === "edit" || event.data.toolName === "create") {
        const p = String(event.data.arguments?.path || "");
        if (p) agentEditPaths.add(resolve(p));
    }
});
session.on("tool.execution_complete", (event) => {
    // Clear after a delay to avoid race with fs.watch
    const p = [...agentEditPaths].find((x) => x); // any tracked path
    setTimeout(() => agentEditPaths.clear(), 3000);
});

const debounce = new Map();

watch(cwd, { recursive: true }, (eventType, filename) => {
    if (!filename || eventType !== "change") return;
    if (filename.split(/[\\\\\\/]/).some((p) => IGNORE.has(p))) return;

    if (debounce.has(filename)) clearTimeout(debounce.get(filename));
    debounce.set(filename, setTimeout(() => {
        debounce.delete(filename);
        const fullPath = join(cwd, filename);
        if (agentEditPaths.has(resolve(fullPath))) return;

        try { if (!statSync(fullPath).isFile()) return; } catch { return; }
        const relPath = relative(cwd, fullPath);
        session.send({
            prompt: `The user edited \\`${relPath}\\`.`,
            attachments: [{ type: "file", path: fullPath }],
        });
    }, 500));
});
```

## Sending Messages Programmatically

### Fire-and-forget

```js
await session.send({ prompt: "Analyze the test results." });
```

### Send and wait for the response

```js
const response = await session.sendAndWait({ prompt: "What is 2 + 2?" });
// response?.data.content contains the agent's reply
```

### Send with file attachments

```js
await session.send({
    prompt: "Review this file",
    attachments: [{ type: "file", path: "./src/index.ts" }],
});
```

---

## Permission and User Input Handlers

### Custom permission logic

```js
const session = await joinSession({
    onPermissionRequest: async (request) => {
        if (request.kind === "shell") {
            // request.fullCommandText has the shell command
            return { kind: "approve-once" };
        }
        if (request.kind === "write") {
            return { kind: "approve-once" };
        }
        return { kind: "reject" };
    },
});
```

### Handling agent questions (ask_user)

Register `onUserInputRequest` to enable the agent's `ask_user` tool:

```js
const session = await joinSession({
    onUserInputRequest: async (request) => {
        // request.question has the agent's question
        // request.choices has the options (if multiple choice)
        return { answer: "yes", wasFreeform: false };
    },
});
```

---

## Complete Example: Multi-Feature Extension

An extension that combines tools, hooks, and events.

```js
import { execFile, exec } from "node:child_process";
import { joinSession } from "@github/copilot-sdk/extension";

const isWindows = process.platform === "win32";
let copyNextResponse = false;

function copyToClipboard(text) {
    const proc = execFile(isWindows ? "clip" : "pbcopy", [], () => {});
    proc.stdin.write(text);
    proc.stdin.end();
}

function openInEditor(filePath) {
    if (isWindows) exec(`code "${filePath}"`, () => {});
    else execFile("code", [filePath], () => {});
}

const session = await joinSession({
    hooks: {
        onUserPromptSubmitted: async (input) => {
            if (/\\bcopy this\\b/i.test(input.prompt)) {
                copyNextResponse = true;
            }
            return {
                additionalContext: "Follow our team style guide. Use 4-space indentation.",
            };
        },
        onPreToolUse: async (input) => {
            if (input.toolName === "bash") {
                const cmd = String(input.toolArgs?.command || "");
                if (/rm\\s+-rf\\s+\//i.test(cmd) || /Remove-Item\\s+.*-Recurse/i.test(cmd)) {
                    return {
                        permissionDecision: "deny",
                        permissionDecisionReason: "Destructive commands are not allowed.",
                    };
                }
            }
        },
        onPostToolUse: async (input) => {
            if (input.toolName === "create" || input.toolName === "edit") {
                const filePath = input.toolArgs?.path;
                if (filePath) openInEditor(filePath);
            }
        },
    },
    tools: [
        {
            name: "copy_to_clipboard",
            description: "Copies text to the system clipboard.",
            parameters: {
                type: "object",
                properties: {
                    text: { type: "string", description: "Text to copy" },
                },
                required: ["text"],
            },
            handler: async (args) => {
                return new Promise((resolve) => {
                    const proc = execFile(isWindows ? "clip" : "pbcopy", [], (err) => {
                        if (err) resolve(`Error: ${err.message}`);
                        else resolve("Copied to clipboard.");
                    });
                    proc.stdin.write(args.text);
                    proc.stdin.end();
                });
            },
        },
    ],
});

session.on("assistant.message", (event) => {
    if (copyNextResponse) {
        copyNextResponse = false;
        copyToClipboard(event.data.content);
    }
});

session.on("tool.execution_complete", (event) => {
    // event.data.success, event.data.result
});
```
````

import type { CopilotSession } from "./session.js";
import { type PermissionHandler, type ResumeSessionConfig } from "./types.js";
import type { FactoryHandle } from "./factory.js";
export { Canvas, CanvasError, createCanvas, type CanvasAction, type CanvasDeclaration, type CanvasHostContext, type CanvasJsonSchema, type CanvasOptions, } from "./canvas.js";
export type JoinSessionConfig = Omit<ResumeSessionConfig, "onPermissionRequest" | "extensionSdkPath"> & {
    onPermissionRequest?: PermissionHandler;
    /**
     * Names of sensitive environment variables this extension needs, such as
     * `"GITHUB_TOKEN"`.
     *
     * The Copilot CLI strips sensitive variables from every extension process
     * before it starts, so an extension that needs one must ask for it by name.
     * The CLI prompts the user with the extension's name and the exact list of
     * variables requested. On approval the granted values are written into this
     * process's `process.env` before {@link joinSession} resolves, so they are
     * readable afterwards. On denial the join rejects and the extension does not
     * load, so its tools never reach the model.
     *
     * An approval is remembered against the exact set of names the user saw, so
     * asking for an additional variable later prompts again. Names that are unset

export interface Tool<TArgs = unknown> {
    name: string;
    description?: string;
    parameters?: ZodSchema<TArgs> | Record<string, unknown>;
    handler?: ToolHandler<TArgs>;
    /**
     * When true, explicitly indicates this tool is intended to override a built-in tool
     * of the same name. If not set and the name clashes with a built-in tool, the runtime
     * will return an error.
     */
    overridesBuiltInTool?: boolean;
    /**
     * When true, the tool can execute without a permission prompt.
     */
    skipPermission?: boolean;
    /**
     * Controls whether the tool may be deferred (loaded lazily via tool search)
     * rather than always pre-loaded. When `"auto"`, the tool can be deferred and
     * surfaced through tool search. When `"never"`, the tool is always pre-loaded.
     * Optional; defaults to `"auto"`.
     */
    defer?: "auto" | "never";
    /**
     * Opaque, host-defined metadata associated with the tool definition.
     *
     * Keys are namespaced and are not part of the stable public API. Values are
     * not interpreted and may be recognized to inform host-specific behavior.
     * Unknown keys are preserved and round-tripped untouched.
     */
    metadata?: Record<string, unknown>;
    /**
     * When true, a successful call to this tool ends the agent turn: the runtime's
     * tool phase halts instead of feeding the tool result back to the model for
     * another round. A failed call (for example input validation) leaves the loop
     * running so the model can read the error and retry.
     *
     * Use this for tools whose whole purpose is to terminate the turn, such as a
     * context clear that replaces the conversation the model would otherwise
     * continue from.
     */
    isTerminal?: boolean;
}

```
> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://resend.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Receiving Emails

> An introduction to receiving emails with Resend.

## Receiving emails through Resend

Resend provides all the tools you need to receive emails (commonly called inbound) at [a verified domain](/docs/dashboard/domains/introduction), or at your account's Resend-managed `<id>.resend.app` subdomain.

This is useful for:

* Receiving support emails from users.
* Processing forwarded attachments.
* Replying to emails from customers.

## Receiving features

With Resend's email receiving features, you can:

* View all received emails in the [**Emails** Dashboard page](https://resend.com/emails).
* Receive incoming emails and [get notified with a webhook](/docs/dashboard/receiving/create-receiving-webhook) event.
* [Poll for new inbound emails in the terminal](/docs/cli#receiving) and display them as they arrive.
* [Retrieve full email content](/docs/dashboard/receiving/get-email-content) (HTML, text, headers) for use in your application.
* [Process attachments](/docs/dashboard/receiving/attachments) using attachment metadata and temporary download URLs.
* [Forward emails](/docs/dashboard/receiving/forward-emails) to another email address.
* [Reply to emails](/docs/dashboard/receiving/reply-to-emails) in the same thread
* [View API endpoint logs](/docs/dashboard/logs/introduction) and deliverability metrics for monitoring and troubleshooting.

## Quickstart

To start receiving emails using a domain managed by Resend, get your unique `<id>.resend.app` domain:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Go to the Emails page in your Resend dashboard." />

  <Step title="Select the Receiving tab." />

  <Step title="Get your custom Resend domain.">
    Click the three dots button and select Receiving address to see your custom Resend subdomain.

    <img alt="Get your Resend domain" src="https://mintcdn.com/resend/stmz8SfTchQy1hpq/images/inbound-resend-domain.jpg?fit=max&auto=format&n=stmz8SfTchQy1hpq&q=85&s=c26fcec3f9dc5def25041d44cb8c501a" width="1159" height="297" data-path="images/inbound-resend-domain.jpg" />
  </Step>

  <Step title="Send yourself a test email.">
    Send an email to any username at your subdomain (e.g., `test@<id>.resend.app`). You will receive emails sent to any address at your Resend domain.
  </Step>

  <Step title="View your received email in the Receiving tab of the Emails Dashboard page." />
</Steps>

You can also [configure a verified domain for receiving emails](/docs/dashboard/receiving/custom-domains) at your custom domain. Once you add the MX record to your custom domain, you will receive emails through Resend for any address at that domain.

## Configure Webhook

Once you can receive mail, you can [create a received mail webhook](/docs/dashboard/receiving/create-receiving-webhook) to receive real-time notifications about incoming email.

Resend processes all incoming emails to your receiving domain, parses the contents and attachments, and then sends a `POST` request to an endpoint that you choose to handle the received email.

<img alt="Receiving email process" src="https://mintcdn.com/resend/bxWCBKtofKnXvbvf/images/receiving-emails.jpeg?fit=max&auto=format&n=bxWCBKtofKnXvbvf&q=85&s=faa9d79f48a43f320d2b5a800256060e" width="1590" height="790" data-path="images/receiving-emails.jpeg" />

## Choose your infrastructure

To handle your received emails, you can use a variety of tools:

* [SDK](/docs/sdks): process inbound emails with an SDK built for your language
* [Integrations](/docs/integrations): process inbound emails using a framework or tool you already use
* [API](/docs/api-reference/emails/retrieve-received-email): process inbound emails with raw HTTP API calls
* [CLI](/docs/cli#receiving): process inbound emails and stream incoming messages from the terminal
* [MCP](/docs/mcp-server): list, read, and download inbound emails through your agent with MCP

See how to use all of Resend's receiving features such as processing attachments and forwarding emails to another address in the [receiving email guides](#related-guides).

## Manage your received emails

After you've received your first email, you'll be able to view and manage your emails in the [Emails Dashboard page](https://resend.com/emails) under the Receiving tab. From here, you can view email details, share a public version, and more.

You can also manage your emails programmatically using the [Receiving API](/docs/api-reference/emails/retrieve-received-email), [CLI commands](/docs/cli#receiving), or the [MCP server](/docs/mcp-server).

Learn more about [managing your received emails](/docs/dashboard/receiving/manage-emails) in the dedicated guide.

## Related Guides

See how to use Resend's receiving features.
```

````
    document.addEventListener('mintlify-localstorage', onStorage);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener('mintlify-localstorage', onStorage);
    };
  }, []);
  const toCamelCase = str => typeof str === 'string' ? str.replace(/[_-](\w)/g, (_, c) => c.toUpperCase()) : str;
  const resolvedBody = useMemo(() => {
    const value = JSON.parse(lang);
    return value === 'Node.js' ? toCamelCase(body) : body;
  }, [body, lang]);
  const resolvedPath = useMemo(() => {
    const value = JSON.parse(lang);
    return value === 'Node.js' ? toCamelCase(path) : path;
  }, [path, lang]);
  return <ParamField body={resolvedBody} path={resolvedPath} {...props}>
      {children}
    </ParamField>;
};

## Body Parameters

<ParamField body="from" type="string" required>
  Sender email address.

  To include a friendly name, pass the sender as `Name <email@example.com>`, for example `Acme <onboarding@example.dev>`.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="to" type="string | string[]" required>
  Recipient email address. For multiple addresses, send as an array of strings.
  Max 50.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="subject" type="string" required>
  Email subject.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="bcc" type="string | string[]">
  Bcc recipient email address. For multiple addresses, send as an array of
  strings.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="cc" type="string | string[]">
  Cc recipient email address. For multiple addresses, send as an array of
  strings.
</ParamField>

<ResendParamField body="scheduled_at" type="string">
  Schedule email to be sent later. The date should be in natural language (e.g.: `in 1 min`) or ISO 8601 format (e.g:
  `2026-08-05T11:52:01.858Z`).

  [See examples](/docs/dashboard/emails/schedule-email)
</ResendParamField>

<ResendParamField body="reply_to" type="string | string[]">
  Reply-to email address. For multiple addresses, send as an array of strings.
</ResendParamField>

<ParamField body="html" type="string">
  The HTML version of the message.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="text" type="string">
  The plain text version of the message.

  <Info>
    If not provided, the HTML will be used to generate a plain text version. You
    can opt out of this behavior by setting value to an empty string.
  </Info>
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="react" type="React.ReactNode">
  The React component used to write the message. *Only available in the Node.js
  SDK.*
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="headers" type="object">
  Custom headers to add to the email.
</ParamField>

<ResendParamField body="topic_id" type="string">
  The topic ID to receive the email.

  * If the recipient is a contact and has opted-in to the topic, the email is sent.
  * If the recipient is a contact and has opted-out of the topic, the email is not sent and will be marked as failed.
  * If the recipient is not a contact, the email is sent if the topic default subscription value is set to `opt-in`.

  <Note>Each email address (to, cc, bcc) is checked and handled separately.</Note>
</ResendParamField>

<ParamField body="attachments" type="array">
  Filename and content of attachments (max 40MB per email, after Base64 encoding of the attachments).

  [See examples](/docs/dashboard/emails/attachments)

  <Expandable defaultOpen title="properties">
    <ParamField body="content" type="buffer | string">
      Content of an attached file, passed as a buffer or Base64 string.
    </ParamField>

    <ParamField body="filename" type="string">
      Name of attached file.
    </ParamField>

    <ParamField body="path" type="string">
      Path where the attachment file is hosted
    </ParamField>

    <ResendParamField body="content_type" type="string">
      Content type for the attachment, if not set will be derived from the filename property
    </ResendParamField>

    <ResendParamField body="content_id" type="string">
      You can embed images using the content id parameter for the attachment. To show the image, you need to include the ID in the `src` attribute of the `img` tag (e.g., `<img src="cid:...">`) of your HTML. [Learn about inline images](/docs/dashboard/emails/embed-inline-images).
    </ResendParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="tags" type="array">
  Custom data passed in key/value pairs.

  [See examples](/docs/dashboard/emails/tags).

  <Expandable defaultOpen title="properties">
    <ParamField body="name" type="string" required>
      The name of the email tag.

      It can only contain ASCII letters (a–z, A–Z), numbers (0–9), underscores (\_), or dashes (-).

      It can contain no more than 256 characters.
    </ParamField>

    <ParamField body="value" type="string" required>
      The value of the email tag.

      It can only contain ASCII letters (a–z, A–Z), numbers (0–9), underscores (\_), or dashes (-).

      It can contain no more than 256 characters.
    </ParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="template" type="object">
  To send using a template, provide a `template` object with:

  * `id`: the id *or* the alias of the published template
  * `variables`: an object with a key for each variable (if applicable)

  <Info>
    If a `template` is provided, you cannot send `html`, `text`, or `react` in the payload, otherwise the API will return a validation error.

    When sending a template, the payload for `from`, `subject`, and `reply_to` take precedence over the template's defaults for these fields. If the template does not provide a default value for these fields, you must provide them in the payload.
  </Info>
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="id" type="string" required>
  The id of the published email template. Required if `template` is provided. Only published templates can be used when sending emails.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="variables" type="object">
  Template variables object with key/value pairs.

  ```ts theme={"theme":{"light":"github-light","dark":"vesper"}}
  variables: {
      CTA: 'Sign up now',
      CTA_LINK: 'https://example.com/signup'
  }
  ```

  When sending the template, the HTML will be parsed. If all the variables used in the template were provided, the email will be sent. If not, the call will throw a validation error.

  See the [errors reference](/docs/api-reference/errors) for more details or [learn more about templates](/docs/dashboard/templates/introduction).

  <Expandable defaultOpen title="properties">
    <ParamField body="key" type="string" required>
      The key of the variable.

      May only contain ASCII letters (a–z, A–Z), numbers (0–9), and underscores (\_). The following variable names are reserved and cannot be used: `FIRST_NAME`, `LAST_NAME`, `EMAIL`, `UNSUBSCRIBE_URL`.

      It can contain no more than 50 characters.
    </ParamField>

    <ParamField body="value" type="string | number" required>
      The value of the variable.

      Observe these technical limitations:

      * `string`: maximum length of 2,000 characters
      * `number`: not greater than 2^53 - 1
    </ParamField>
  </Expandable>
</ParamField>
````

### Copilot

Verification complete against the installed SDK at `C:\Users\jeffkramer\.copilot\pkg\win32-x64\1.0.83-3\copilot-sdk`. The core architecture holds: `joinSession`, custom tools, `onPermissionRequest`, `session.send({mode:"enqueue"})`, `session.log`, and the `assistant.message` / `user.message` / `session.idle` / `session.error` / `session.shutdown` events all exist in 1.0.83-3. Remaining issues below.

---

## BLOCKER

None.

## HIGH

**H1 — "Owner-only Windows named pipe" is not achievable in Node; the claim is empirically false.**
*Sections:* "Trust and safety boundaries" ("Use an owner-only Windows named pipe rather than a loopback TCP port"); "Copilot extension" ("owner-only Windows named pipe").
I created a Node `net.createServer().listen('\\\\.\\pipe\\…')` and read its DACL:

```
D:(A;;FA;;;SY)(A;;FA;;;BA)(A;;FA;;;<creator>)(A;;FR;;;WD)(A;;FR;;;AN)
```

`FR` to `WD` (Everyone) and `AN` (Anonymous). libuv passes `NULL` security attributes to `CreateNamedPipeW` and exposes no way to set an SD, so any local process can connect and read frames containing question text, email bodies, and answers. The stated rationale for preferring pipes over loopback TCP evaporates.
*Fix (≈20 lines):* drop the "owner-only" wording; add a per-run handshake. Daemon generates a 128-bit secret, writes it to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\amail\bridge.token` with an owner-only file ACL (which *is* achievable), and closes any connection whose first frame isn't that secret. Send nothing to a connection before the handshake succeeds. State the residual risk in the README.

**H2 — Mandatory `In-Reply-To` matching will likely reject every legitimate reply.**
*Sections:* "Resend integration" ("A reply must also reference the recorded outbound message ID through `In-Reply-To`"); "Trust and safety boundaries" ("Reject … replies that do not match the expected outbound `Message-ID`").
Resend's send response returns Resend's own `id`, not the RFC 5322 `Message-ID`. Custom `headers` are supported, but whether a caller-supplied `Message-ID` survives Resend's MTA is unverified, and mail clients rewrite/omit `In-Reply-To` inconsistently. As written this is a hard authorization gate on a value you may never learn.
*Fix:* demote to advisory. The token already is the capability. Change to: "If the recorded outbound `Message-ID` is known and the reply's `In-Reply-To`/`References` contradicts it, log and reject; a missing header is not a rejection." Keep exact-sender match + single-use token as the two mandatory checks.

**H3 — A blocked `ask_human_by_email` handler cannot be cancelled by the runtime; the session can wedge.**
*Sections:* "Copilot extension"; "Failure behavior" ("Tool or permission request cancelled"); "Important unknowns to validate early".
Verified: tool calls arrive as an `external_tool.requested` **broadcast event** (`extension.js` `_handleBroadcastEvent`), and `ToolInvocation` (`types.d.ts:446`) carries only `sessionId`/`toolCallId`/`toolName`/`arguments` — **no `AbortSignal`, no cancellation callback**. Nothing tells a pending handler that the user pressed Esc. With a 24-hour expiry as the only bound, a wedged turn means restarting the CLI mid-demo.
*Fix (all three, ≈30 lines):*
1. Subscribe to `external_tool.requested` and build a `toolCallId → requestId` map, because the handler never sees `requestId`. Then treat `external_tool.completed` (payload is `{requestId}`) for that request as cancellation: expire the token, resolve the pending promise, stop waiting.
2. Also self-cancel on root `session.idle` with `aborted: true` and on `session.shutdown`.
3. Give the tool its own bounded wait (recommend 15–30 min, configurable) that is far shorter than the 24h token TTL, and on expiry **return a string** like `"No email answer received within N minutes."` rather than hanging — the model can then end the turn cleanly.

**H4 — Email permission handling has no "away" gate, so it hijacks every prompt.**
*Sections:* "When Copilot needs permission"; "Copilot extension" (`implements onPermissionRequest`).
`onPermissionRequest` fires for *every* permission request, including while the user is sitting at the terminal. "The extension handles permission requests while the user is away" is never operationalized — there is no presence signal in the SDK. Without a gate you either email every `bash` approval or the behavior is undefined.
*Fix:* add an explicit armed/away flag owned by the daemon (set via a daemon CLI subcommand, mirroring the existing `STOP` command). When not armed, the handler returns `{ kind: "no-result" }` **immediately** — verified at `extension.js:7833`, a `no-result` handler sends no RPC response, so the TUI prompt proceeds untouched. Document that this, not presence detection, is the boundary.

## MEDIUM

**M1 — `session.send` delivery confirmation has no supported correlation key.**
*Sections:* "State machine" ("matching `user.message` confirms delivery"); "Local daemon".
`SendResult.messageId` exists, but the generated `UserMessageData` (`session-events.d.ts:3143`) has **no `messageId` field** — the runtime emits one, but it is untyped and unsupported. `SendRequest` also has no `source` field, so injected prompts are indistinguishable from typed ones (the CLI's own root-turn filter is `agentId === undefined && data.source === undefined`).
*Fix:* state the correlation rule explicitly: single outstanding delivery per session + exact `event.data.content` match against the injected prompt (or `displayPrompt`, which is what the event carries when set). Opportunistically read the untyped `messageId` as a bonus, never as the sole key.

**M2 — Queued delivery may not confirm for a long time; don't let that trigger a retry.**
*Section:* "State machine" (`DeliveryPending --> Running`).
`UserMessageDelivery` is `"idle" | "steering" | "queued"`, and the CLI emits `user.message` immediately only for `steering`; an `enqueue`d message is surfaced when its turn actually starts. So `DeliveryPending` legitimately persists for the whole in-flight turn.
*Fix:* add "`DeliveryPending` has no timeout; it clears only on `user.message`, `session.shutdown`, or explicit cancellation. The daemon must never re-inject a prompt that `session.send()` accepted." Also note that `delivery === "queued"` means accepted-not-running, so the state name `Running` is reached at dequeue, not at send.

**M3 — Root filtering discriminator is unnamed.**
*Sections:* "When Copilot completes"; "Failure behavior" ("Sub-agent events: ignore them").
The SDK is explicit: every event carries `agentId?` — *"Absent for events from the root/main agent and session-level events."*
*Fix:* one sentence: "Root events are those with `event.agentId === undefined`; this is the same predicate the CLI uses internally for root user turns."

**M4 — "The agent's final response" can arrive as several `assistant.message` events.**
*Section:* "When Copilot completes".
`AssistantMessageData` carries `chunkIndex`/`chunkCount` — *"Total messages the model call's response was split into, one per reasoning boundary."* Capturing only the last `assistant.message` before idle will email a fragment.
*Fix:* buffer all root `assistant.message` events since the last root `assistant.turn_start` and join them in order; reset the buffer on each `turn_start`.

**M5 — Permission handling has the same TUI race the design cites as its reason for rejecting `ask_user` interception.**
*Sections:* "Alternatives considered" (Native `ask_user` interception row); "When Copilot needs permission".
`permission.requested` is broadcast to both the TUI and the extension; first responder wins and the loser gets "tool approval was resolved by another client" (benign, logged at debug). The race is real but harmless — the rationale row is just internally inconsistent, and the concrete dismissal mechanism is missing.
*Fix:* reword the Alternatives row to cite the actual differentiators (session-level variant selection, orphaned callbacks on reload) and add to the extension bullet list: "subscribes to `permission.completed` (payload `{requestId, result, toolCallId?}`) to expire the email token when the TUI or policy resolves the request first."

**M6 — Windows has no SIGTERM; don't rely on graceful extension shutdown.**
*Sections:* "Why a foreground extension"; "Failure behavior" (Extension reload / CLI exit).
The SDK docs' "SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5s" is POSIX phrasing; on Windows the child is terminated abruptly and `process.on("SIGTERM")` cleanup will not run.
*Fix:* state that cleanup is driven by the `session.shutdown` event when it arrives, and otherwise by the daemon detecting pipe closure — never by a signal handler.

## LOW

**L1 — Prune the "Important unknowns" list.** These are now resolved and shouldn't consume spike time: extensions load by default (config default is `extensions.mode = "load_and_augment"`; no per-extension trust prompt exists, only the env-var prompt, which `amail` doesn't need since the key stays in the daemon); permission response shapes are the `PermissionDecisionRequest["result"]` union — `{kind:"approve-once"}`, `{kind:"reject"}` (optional `feedback`), plus the SDK-only `{kind:"no-result"}` pass-through; cancellation is surfaced only as described in H3; Resend's managed domain accepts **any** local-part at `<id>.resend.app`, so `reply+<token>@…` routing is confirmed viable. Keep only the Resend account-state and inbound-auth-verdict unknowns.

**L2 — `session.idle` is `ephemeral: true`.** It is never persisted to the session event log, so a daemon that restarts across an idle transition cannot recover it from history. Worth one line in "Daemon restart": missed idle events are lost, not replayed.

**L3 — Untapped affordance, optional.** `SendRequest` supports `wait?: boolean` via `session.rpc.session.send(...)`, and `Tool.handler` may be omitted in favor of resolving through `session.tools.handlePendingToolCall({requestId, result|error})`. The latter is a cleaner cancellation story than a blocking handler, but it is more machinery than 3–5 hours warrants — mention as future work only.

---

Not SATISFIED — H1–H4 remain. All four are wording-plus-small-code changes (roughly 60–80 lines total across the extension and daemon) and none disturb the architecture, so the plan is implementable within budget once they land.

### Copilot

I re-investigated the native path directly in the 1.0.83-3 runtime rather than trusting the design's rejection. The design has it **backwards**: native user-input handling is the *more* lifecycle-robust of the two mechanisms.

## What the runtime actually does

- `user_input.requested` carries `{requestId, question, choices?, allowFreeform?, toolCallId?}` and is **broadcast to every attached client**. The TUI is just another subscriber — I found it registering `["user_input.requested","user_input.completed","elicitation.requested","elicitation.completed"]` through the same `session.on()` API an extension uses.
- Resolution is an explicit **compare-and-swap**: `session.rpc.ui.handlePendingUserInput({requestId, response:{answer, wasFreeform}})` → `{success: boolean}`, documented as false when "already resolved by another client, expired, or otherwise no longer pending."
- Cancellation is a **first-class typed event**: `user_input.completed {requestId, answer?, wasFreeform?}`. `settleTurn()` cancels every pending input request when a turn ends; abort additionally emits `session.idle {aborted:true}`. Permissions get the same treatment with `permission.completed` carrying `result:{kind:"cancelled", reason:...}`.
- **No suppression mechanism exists** for user input or permissions. Only `auto_mode_switch` has `registerDirectAutoModeSwitchHandler`, whose docs say registration "tells the server bridge to skip its own dispatch so a remote client doesn't race the in-process handler." Its absence for `user_input` is deliberate: racing peers is the supported model.

Contrast the custom tool: `ToolInvocation` has **no AbortSignal**, the handler never receives `requestId` (only `toolCallId`), `external_tool.completed` carries only `requestId`, and on extension reload the in-flight promise dies with **nothing else able to answer** — the turn hangs permanently.

## UX robustness vs lifecycle robustness

**Lifecycle robustness** — can the request be resolved exactly once, learn of cancellation, and survive reload? Native **wins decisively**. All state lives in the runtime keyed by `requestId`; the extension holds no callback, so reload is a correctness no-op and the TUI can still answer. The custom tool holds the only callback and orphans it.

**UX robustness** — does the human still get a sane terminal experience, and the agent a well-shaped answer? Native is **weaker but adequate**, and its failure mode is fail-safe: if the extension does nothing, the TUI behaves exactly as today. The custom tool's failure mode is fail-hang. Native's real UX cost is thinner email content — `ask_user` gives you `question` + `choices` only, with no subject or context, versus the tool's `{subject, questions[], context}`.

## Smallest hardened design

Collapse all four flows into **one** `PendingRequest` record; the native path then costs a third `kind`, not a third subsystem.

```
PendingRequest {
  id, sessionId, kind: "tool_question"|"native_question"|"permission"|"followup",
  runtimeRequestId?, turnId?, tokenHash, expiresAt, status, outboundMessageId,
  constraints?: { choices?: string[], allowFreeform: boolean }
}
```

Five hazards, five rules:

1. **First-responder-wins.** Consume the token atomically, *then* call the CAS. `success:false` ⇒ mark superseded, never retry, optionally send a one-line "answered at the terminal" note. Two independent gates (single-use token + CAS) mean a stale reply can neither answer a different request nor double-answer the same one.
2. **Cancellation/abort.** Subscribe to `user_input.completed` and `permission.completed`; on arrival for a tracked `requestId`, expire the token and stop waiting. Sweep by `turnId` on root `session.idle {aborted:true}`.
3. **Reload.** Native input and permissions survive reload in the runtime; only the custom tool orphans. On restart, re-adopt pending permissions via `session.rpc.permissions.pendingRequests()` (this RPC exists). **There is no equivalent listing for user input** — so after reload a pending native question simply stays answerable at the terminal only. Say so explicitly rather than claiming recovery.
4. **Variant constraints.** Do **not** pass `onUserInputRequest` or `askUserVariant` to `joinSession`. Both flow into the `session.resume` payload (`requestUserInput`, `askUserVariant`), and the runtime resolves the variant at create/cold-resume via `sessionScalarResolveAskUserVariant(...)`, merely logging a warning when it can't honor a late request. Subscribe to the event and use the CAS instead — this touches no session-level state. Note also that the SDK's `_handleBroadcastEvent` has branches for `external_tool.requested`, `permission.requested`, `elicitation.requested` and others but **none for `user_input.requested`**, so `onUserInputRequest` would not fire for a joined extension anyway.
5. **Answer shape.** Validate the reply against `choices`/`allowFreeform` before the CAS. Exact choice match ⇒ `{answer: <matched choice>, wasFreeform: false}`. No match and `allowFreeform === false` ⇒ **do not answer**; reply-mail the valid choices and keep waiting. Otherwise ⇒ `{answer: <cleaned body>, wasFreeform: true}`. If the session resolved to the `elicitation` variant, `user_input.requested` never fires — detect at preflight and no-op.

## Keep both? Yes — but re-sequence

Justified, because the incremental cost is genuinely small (~60–90 lines) *once the shared `PendingRequest` machine exists*, and the two cover different needs: the custom tool gives rich, deliberate, demo-deterministic check-ins and is what makes `amail` an agent interface; native handling covers spontaneous questions from tools and skills you don't control, which is the actual "walk away and it just works" claim. Rejecting native outright leaves a hole the take-home's own premise advertises.

Revise the implementation slice to **4) `ask_human_by_email` → 5) native `user_input` (reuses the question email format + adds answer-shape validation) → 6) permissions (strictest parsing, highest blast radius) → 7) tests → 8) `--simulate-inbound`.** This moves the cut-line onto *permissions* rather than native input, which is the correct risk posture: email-approving shell commands is the scariest feature, not the most essential one.

## Findings

**HIGH**

- **H1 — Named pipe is not owner-only.** Unchanged from earlier this round. Measured DACL on a Node pipe: `(A;;FR;;;WD)(A;;FR;;;AN)` — Everyone and Anonymous get read. Drop the claim; add a 128-bit handshake secret in an owner-ACL'd file under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\amail\`.
- **H2 — Mandatory `In-Reply-To` match will reject legitimate replies.** Unchanged. Resend's send response returns its own `id`, not the RFC 5322 `Message-ID`. Demote to advisory; the token is the capability.
- **H3 — Custom-tool cancellation (revised).** Still a real defect, but now also the strongest argument *for* the native path. Fix as previously described (map `toolCallId`→`requestId` from `external_tool.requested`, watch `external_tool.completed`, self-cancel on aborted root idle, bounded wait that **returns a string** instead of hanging).
- **H4 — No "away" gate.** Now applies to all three interception paths. Add a daemon-owned armed flag; when unarmed, return `{kind:"no-result"}` for permissions and simply don't call the CAS for user input. Both are verified fail-safe: the TUI proceeds untouched.
- **H5 — "Alternatives considered" rejects native `ask_user` on three grounds that are all false.** *Section:* Alternatives table, row 1. "TUI and extension race to resolve the same pending request" — the race is the supported model, arbitrated by a documented CAS. "Variant selection is session-level" — true, but irrelevant once you stop passing `askUserVariant`. "Reload can orphan the callback" — backwards; the callback-orphaning path is the custom tool. *Fix:* replace the row with "Choose (hardened)" and record the CAS + `*.completed` mechanism.

**MEDIUM** — M1 (no supported `messageId` on `user.message`; correlate by exact `content` + single outstanding delivery), M2 (queued sends don't emit `user.message` until dequeue; never retry), M3 (name the root filter `event.agentId === undefined`), M4 (buffer all root `assistant.message` chunks since `assistant.turn_start`; `chunkIndex`/`chunkCount` mean the reply can arrive split), M5 (subscribe to `permission.completed` to expire tokens), M6 (no SIGTERM on Windows; drive cleanup from `session.shutdown` and pipe closure) — all carried forward unchanged, plus new **M7**: document the reload asymmetry — permissions re-adoptable, user input not, tool calls orphaned.

**LOW** — L1 (prune resolved unknowns: extensions load by default at `extensions.mode = "load_and_augment"` with no trust prompt; permission result union is `{kind:"approve-once"}` / `{kind:"reject"}` / `{kind:"no-result"}`; Resend's managed domain accepts any local-part, so `reply+<token>@…` routing is confirmed), L2 (`session.idle` is `ephemeral: true` and never replayed after a daemon restart), L3 (`SendRequest.wait` and `handlePendingToolCall` exist as future-work affordances).

---

**Verdict: not SATISFIED.** H1, H2, H4 and H5 remain open, and H3 needs its bounded-wait fix. None are architectural — they are wording changes plus roughly 80–120 lines across the extension and daemon, and the unified `PendingRequest` model makes the native path additive rather than a fourth subsystem. Once those land, the plan is implementable in 3–5 hours **with** both surfaces, and it is a materially stronger take-home for keeping the native path than for cutting it.
